traveler: Lorenzo di Piero de' Medici (Lorenzo il Magnifico)
title: The House on Via Larga: the Banker Who Governed Without an Office
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The House on the Via Larga

stops.name: Via Larga, the casa vecchia and the birth
stops.date_confidence: Date and city attested (Wikipedia, 'Lorenzo de' Medici'; Ingeborg Walter in the Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani). Pin corrected: the family lived in the old house, the casa vecchia, on Via Larga until about 1458, some fifty metres north of the Palazzo Medici Riccardi whose coordinates are usually given for this event.
stops.campa: On the first day of the year a son is born to Piero di Cosimo de' Medici and Lucrezia Tornabuoni in the old house on Via Larga. The new palace Michelozzo is raising for the family stands unfinished fifty metres down the same street, and the boy will move into it before he is ten. His grandfather Cosimo governs Florence without holding any office, through the bank, the marriages and the debts owed to him. It is an inheritance that exists nowhere on paper. Nothing in the constitution of the republic names the family, and there is no title for the child to be given.
sources: Ingeborg Walter, 'Medici, Lorenzo de'', Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani
suggested_refs: The site of the Medici casa vecchia on Via Larga, about fifty metres north of the Palazzo Medici Riccardi

stops.name: Baptistery of San Giovanni, the font at Epiphany
stops.date_confidence: [R] on the day. Florentine practice baptized infants within days of birth and Epiphany is the date carried in the research pool's basic-facts table, but no fetched source states it, so the day is reconstruction rather than attestation. Coordinate corrected to the Baptistery, 43.7731/11.2550; the value 11.2560 circulating for this event is the Cathedral, about eighty metres east.
stops.campa: Five days old, he is carried the short distance to the octagon of San Giovanni and dipped in the font where every Florentine is made a Christian and entered in the city's register of souls. He is named Lorenzo, for the saint whose basilica the Medici have been rebuilding since his great-grandfather's day and in whose sacristy his grandfather will be buried. The party goes in and out past Ghiberti's east doors, gilded, four years in place, on the side of the building that faces the cathedral.
sources: Research pool basic-facts table, drawing on Florentine baptismal-register practice
suggested_refs: The baptismal registers of San Giovanni, Florence, for January 1449

stops.name: Cafaggiolo, the Mugello summers
stops.date_confidence: [R] Reconstruction. The Medici villa at Cafaggiolo in Barberino di Mugello is the family's fortified country seat and standard accounts place Lorenzo's boyhood among the estate villas, but no fetched source documents specific years and the research pool does not name Cafaggiolo. Coordinate corrected to 43.9647/11.2952; the value 43.9989/11.3132 in circulation falls about four kilometres north-east, in open country.
stops.campa: North of Florence, where the Sieve runs down through the Mugello, the family keeps the ground it came from. Cafaggiolo is a farm with battlements, an old castle that Michelozzo squared into a villa without taking the walls away. Here the boy learns to ride and to hunt, and here he meets the tenants, the priests and the notaries of the countryside his family has been buying back parish by parish. A banker's grandson is raised, some months of the year, as a landlord among his own contadini. The moat is still full.
sources: F. W. Kent, Lorenzo de' Medici and the Art of Magnificence
suggested_refs: The Villa medicea di Cafaggiolo, Barberino di Mugello

stops.name: Palazzo Medici, the death of Cosimo
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year only (Wikipedia, 'Lorenzo de' Medici'); month and day defaulted to 01 because the research pool carries no finer date.
stops.campa: Cosimo dies, and the city that never elected him buries him as Pater Patriae, a title voted by the Signoria and cut into the pavement of San Lorenzo. Piero, gouty and cautious, inherits a bank, a party and no office at all. Lorenzo is fifteen and has already been used as a family emissary. He watches the succession happen. There is no crown and no oath. The same men arrive at the same door on Via Larga with the same requests, addressed now to his father.
suggested_refs: Cosimo de' Medici's tomb slab before the high altar of San Lorenzo, inscribed Pater Patriae

segments.name: The Boy Sent to Look at Princes

stops.name: Castello Sforzesco, the Sforza court
stops.date_confidence: The circuit is attested for 1465-1466 (Wikipedia, 'Lorenzo de' Medici'; Rubinstein on the early missions). The individual legs are undated, so month and day default to 01 and the order used here follows the itinerary as listed, not a documented sequence.
stops.campa: Piero, who can barely walk, sends his son to be seen. At Milan the boy stands in the court of the Sforza, condottieri who made themselves dukes and whose alliance with Cosimo has held the peninsula quiet for fifteen years. The Medici bank keeps a branch in the city and the duke owes it money; the two facts are one fact. Lorenzo is sixteen and has nothing to negotiate. He stands where he is put, in a hall got ready for the visit, and is looked at by men his father deals with by letter.
sources: Nicolai Rubinstein on the Medici diplomatic missions
suggested_refs: The Milan branch ledgers of the Medici bank

stops.name: Ferrara, the court of the Este
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a stop on the 1465-1466 circuit (research pool, 'Early Career and Journeys'). Month and day defaulted to 01; the leg is not separately dated.
stops.campa: At Ferrara the Este keep a court famous for horses, poets and a library, holding a marquisate on the Po that Venice covets and the papacy claims the right to grant. The Florentine boy is received with the courtesy owed to his father's money. He is shown the stables and the library. What a small state does in order to remain a state is on display all week: entertainments, the borrowed prestige of scholars, a balance kept by hand between two larger neighbours.
suggested_refs: The Este library and studio at Ferrara in the reign of Borso d'Este

stops.name: Doge's Palace, received in Venice
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a stop on the 1465-1466 circuit (research pool). Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The Republic that Florence half admires and wholly distrusts receives him in the palace on the lagoon, where the Great Council sits and no single family is allowed to become what the Medici already are. Within a year Venice will be backing the attempt to unseat his father. Lorenzo comes as a merchant's son to the greatest merchant city in Europe and is shown the arsenal, the fleet and the constitution: a machine built precisely to prevent a man like his grandfather.
suggested_refs: The Venetian Arsenal and the constitution of the Maggior Consiglio

stops.name: Bologna, the city held without a title
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a stop on the 1465-1466 circuit (research pool). Month and day defaulted to 01. Nothing of the visit's content is recorded in any source reached for this file.
stops.campa: Bologna belongs to the Pope in law and to the Bentivoglio in fact, who hold it as the Medici hold Florence, without a title and without a crown. The city sits astride the road from Florence to the north, and whoever is friendly there decides whether an army can cross the Apennines. Lorenzo is received among men solving his family's problem by his family's methods, in a smaller room. The record gives the city on the itinerary and nothing at all of what was said in it.
suggested_refs: The Bentivoglio regime at Bologna and its relations with Florence

stops.name: Vatican Palace, the first sight of the curia
stops.date_confidence: Rome attested on the 1465-1466 circuit (Wikipedia, 'Lorenzo de' Medici'). Coordinate corrected to the Apostolic Palace, 41.9038/12.4558; the value 41.9029/12.4534 in circulation is St Peter's, about 215 metres south-west. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The Medici are the papacy's bankers, holding the deposits of the Apostolic Chamber and farming the alum of Tolfa. Lorenzo enters the palace as a client of the largest single account in the bank's books. He looks at the cardinals, the notaries, and the Orsini and Colonna men waiting their turn in the antechambers. One office at the end of the corridor can excommunicate a debtor and dissolve every contract he holds, and no ledger in Florence can answer it.
suggested_refs: The Tolfa alum concession and the Medici bank's Rome branch

stops.name: Castel Nuovo, the Aragonese court
stops.date_confidence: Attested as the southern end of the 1465-1466 circuit (research pool). Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The last stop is the kingdom in the south, where Ferrante of Aragon has spent his reign putting down barons and outlasting French claimants. The Castel Nuovo has a triumphal arch cut into the gate between two round towers and a hall in which, it is said, the king has entertained men and arrested them at the table. Lorenzo is a guest of sixteen with nothing to negotiate. He will come back into this room alone at thirty, with his city under two armies, and stake his life on knowing how the man behind the table thinks.
suggested_refs: The Arco di Trionfo of Alfonso of Aragon at the Castel Nuovo, Naples

stops.name: Palazzo Medici, the coup against Piero
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year (Wikipedia, 'Lorenzo de' Medici'); month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Luca Pitti, Dietisalvi Neroni and Niccolò Soderini move against the gouty heir, with Venetian backing promised on the border and armed men gathering in the city. Lorenzo, seventeen, carries the family's messages. The plot fails. The Medici party holds the Signoria, the conspirators are exiled rather than killed, and Pitti is left alive in the enormous half-finished palace he built to outface Cosimo's. Florence has tried once to be rid of them and failed inside a year, without an execution.
suggested_refs: The unfinished Palazzo Pitti as Luca Pitti left it in 1466

stops.name: Piazza Santa Croce, the giostra
stops.date_confidence: The joust and the first prize are attested (Wikipedia, 'Lorenzo de' Medici'), as are Verrocchio's banner and the horse Morello di Vento. The day 7 February is attached in that article to the BETROTHAL rather than to the joust, so the date is carried here at low confidence. CORRECTION of a misattribution in the research pool: Poliziano's Stanze per la giostra celebrate Giuliano's tournament of 1475, not this one; the poem for Lorenzo's giostra is Luigi Pulci's La Giostra. Coordinate tightened to 43.7689/11.2615.
stops.campa: Twenty years old, he rides in the square before Santa Croce under a banner painted by Verrocchio, on a horse called Morello di Vento, and takes the first prize: a helmet worked in silver with a figure of Mars for the crest. He also keeps the accounts. Ten thousand florins went on the day, and he sets the figure down years later without apology, the way a man notes an investment. Luigi Pulci puts the giostra into verse. Machiavelli, a generation later, records that the prize was given for skill at arms and not as a favour.
stops.quote: That I might take part in everything, and bear me like the rest, I did tilt in the Piazza of Santa Croce ... and although I was very vigorous neither of my years nor of blows, yet was the first prize awarded unto me, namely, a helmet adorned with silver and having a figure of Mars for the crest.
stops.quote_source: Lorenzo de' Medici, Ricordi (c. 1483-1485), tr. Mary C. Steegmann in Isidoro Del Lungo, Women of Florence (1907); ellipsis marks an omitted clause
sources: Wikiquote, 'Lorenzo de' Medici', citing Del Lungo, Women of Florence
Niccolò Machiavelli, The Florentine History, vol. 2 (1906 ed.), p. 169
suggested_refs: Luigi Pulci, La Giostra di Lorenzo de' Medici
Verrocchio's lost joust banner of 1469

stops.name: Palazzo Medici, the Orsini marriage
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Wikipedia, 'Clarice Orsini': married 4 June 1469, with a four-day celebration). The six thousand florin dowry comes from the research pool's dossier and was not re-verified against a primary source.
stops.campa: Clarice Orsini, daughter of Jacopo Orsini of Monterotondo, is married into the house with four days of public feasting on Via Larga. She brings six thousand florins and something the Medici cannot buy in Florence: a Roman baronial name, castles in the Campagna, cardinals among the cousins. No Florentine family is slighted by the match, because no Florentine family was chosen over another. Lorenzo's mother made the arrangement. Clarice will bear him ten children and never be entirely at home in the city.
sources: Research pool on the Orsini match and the dowry
suggested_refs: The Orsini holdings at Monterotondo and Bracciano

stops.name: Palazzo Medici, the men who come to the door
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Wikipedia, 'Lorenzo de' Medici', which dates the assumption of power to 2 December 1469; research pool, 'Early Career and Journeys').
stops.campa: Piero dies five months after the wedding. Within two days the leading men of the party come to the house and ask his sons to take up what their father held. Lorenzo is twenty, Giuliano sixteen. There is no office to assume and no vote to hold: the request itself is the whole constitutional act. He accepts. What the record preserves is a delegation arriving at a private door. Nothing about the arrangement is written into law, then or in the twenty-three years that follow.
suggested_refs: The Medici party lists (accoppiatori and the a mano scrutinies) of 1469

stops.name: Prato, the rising of Bernardo Nardi
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year in the research pool, drawn from Florentine political history rather than a source refetched in this pass; consistent with standard accounts of the 1470 Prato revolt but not primary-verified. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: An exile named Bernardo Nardi rides into Prato before dawn with a small band, seizes the podestà in his own palace and calls the town out for its liberty. Prato does not rise. The regime in Florence is one year old and its head is twenty-one, and the thing it most needs to know is whether a subject town will move for a name and a shout in the street. This one does not. Nardi is caught the same morning, tried, and executed, and the whole rising is finished inside a day.
suggested_refs: The Palazzo Pretorio of Prato, seat of the Florentine podesta seized by Nardi

stops.name: Vatican Palace, Sixtus IV newly elected
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year in the research pool from a dossier summary, not re-verified against a primary source. Sixtus IV was elected 9 August 1471 (Wikipedia, 'Pope Sixtus IV'), so the embassy falls in the autumn; month and day are defaulted to 01 because the pool carries only the year. Coordinate corrected to the Apostolic Palace.
stops.campa: Francesco della Rovere is crowned Sixtus IV, Florence sends an embassy, and Lorenzo goes at its head. The reception is warm. The Medici keep the papal deposits and the alum, and honours and commercial advantages are handed out. He is twenty-two, and the pope who will excommunicate him in seven years is at this moment doing him favours. He goes home with antiquities bought in the city, the beginning of a collection he will spend the rest of his life adding to.
suggested_refs: The antique cameos and hardstone vases acquired by Lorenzo at Rome, later inventoried in the Medici collection

stops.name: Basilica di San Lorenzo, the ledger and the library
stops.date_confidence: The 663,755-florin reckoning is Lorenzo's own, recorded in the Ricordi and covering the years 1434 to 1471. Patronage of San Lorenzo and the descent of the family library into the Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana are attested in the research pool. The year on this stop is the year of the reckoning, not of a single event; month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The parish church of the family is also its account book. Since 1434 the Medici have laid out six hundred and sixty-three thousand seven hundred and fifty-five florins on buildings, charities and taxes, and Lorenzo, totting the sum up, declares it well spent and himself well pleased. Under the same roof stands the library Cosimo assembled, manuscripts bought out of Byzantium and out of ruined abbeys, which Lorenzo keeps adding to and keeps lending out. He counts the books among the expenditure, and the expenditure among the honour of the state.
stops.quote: I do not regret this for though many would consider it better to have a part of that sum in their purse, I consider it to have been a great honour to our state, and I think the money was well-expended and I am well-pleased.
stops.quote_source: Lorenzo de' Medici, Ricordi, on 663,755 florins spent between 1434 and 1471; tr. in G. Brucker (ed.), The Society of Renaissance Florence: A Documentary Study (1971), p. 27
sources: G. Brucker (ed.), The Society of Renaissance Florence (1971), p. 27
suggested_refs: The Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana and the surviving Medici manuscript inventories

stops.name: Piazza dei Priori, Volterra sacked
stops.date_confidence: Siege dates and the sack are attested (Wikipedia, 'Volterra'). Responsibility is contested and is not resolved here: the research pool stresses that no direct order to pillage is established, and frames Lorenzo's part at the level of policy, his regime having pressed for the intervention and profited by it.
stops.campa: A dispute over an alum vein under Volterra turns into a question of who governs a subject city. Florence sends Federico da Montefeltro. After twenty-five days the town surrenders on terms, and two days later the soldiers sack it anyway, house by house. No order of his to pillage has ever been produced, and he rides out afterwards with money for the ruined and instructions for the rebuilding. Volterra stays Florentine. Florence then builds a fortress on the hill above the town.
sources: Research pool summary of the 1472 Volterra episode
suggested_refs: The Fortezza Nuova at Volterra, built by Florence after the sack

stops.name: Pisa, the archbishop Florence will not have
stops.date_confidence: The Salviati dispute is carried in the research pool as one of the linked quarrels of 1474-1478 and was not re-verified against a primary source in this pass. Month and day defaulted to 01; the stop is dated to the opening of the quarrel, not to a single day.
stops.campa: Sixtus names Francesco Salviati archbishop of Pisa. Pisa is Florentine ground, and Florence holds that no archbishop is seated there without its consent. Lorenzo keeps him out. The quarrel joins the others piling up: the alum, the loan for Imola that the Medici refused and the Pazzi bank made, the papal deposits moved off Via Larga. Four years of refused courtesies and paperwork accumulate between Via Larga and the curia. Salviati is still being kept out of Pisa in the spring of 1478.
sources: Research pool, '1473-1477: Banking strain, papal rupture and cultural statecraft'
suggested_refs: The archiepiscopal see of Pisa and the Florentine right of consent

stops.name: Santa Maria del Fiore, the elevation of the Host
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Wikipedia, 'Pazzi conspiracy'). CORRECTION of a claim carried in the research pool: this was NOT Easter Sunday. Easter 1478 fell on 22 March; 26 April was an ordinary Sunday in late April. The Italian account gives the hour as about 13:30. Attack during High Mass, Giuliano stabbed to death, Lorenzo wounded in the neck, escape into the sacristy, and the death of Francesco Nori are all confirmed.
stops.campa: High Mass, the cathedral full, the bells sounding at the elevation. Francesco de' Pazzi and Bernardo Bandini Baroncelli fall on Giuliano and stab him to death on the floor of the church. Two others take Lorenzo from behind and open his neck. He turns, gets his cloak round his arm, vaults the choir rail and reaches the north sacristy, and the bronze doors are dragged shut behind him. Francesco Nori dies in the doorway covering him. At the same hour Archbishop Salviati is across the city trying to take the government palace, and failing.
suggested_refs: Luca della Robbia's bronze sacristy doors at Santa Maria del Fiore, shut behind Lorenzo

stops.name: Palazzo della Signoria, the windows
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Wikipedia, 'Pazzi conspiracy'). CORRECTION of the date range carried in the research pool: Salviati and Francesco de' Pazzi were hanged from the windows within hours of the attack on 26 April, but Jacopo de' Pazzi on 28 April, at the twenty-third hour, per it.wikipedia, 'Congiura dei Pazzi'. The bodies thrown into the Arno is confirmed by that source; the detail of their being dragged through the streets is carried as tradition only.
stops.campa: Within hours Archbishop Francesco Salviati is hanging from a window of the government palace in his vestments, and Francesco de' Pazzi beside him, stripped, bleeding from the thigh he stabbed by accident in the cathedral. The window is on the front of the building where the republic keeps its laws. Two days later Jacopo de' Pazzi is brought back from the hills and hanged from the same row at the twenty-third hour. The bodies are cut down and thrown into the Arno.
suggested_refs: The window range on the Via dei Gondi front of the Palazzo Vecchio

stops.name: Rome, the bull of excommunication
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Wikipedia, 'Pazzi conspiracy': Sixtus IV issued a bull excommunicating Lorenzo and his supporters on 1 June 1478). Lorenzo was in Florence; the pin marks the curia that issued the bull and not a place he stood.
stops.campa: Sixtus IV, whose nephew's circle has just failed to kill him, excommunicates Lorenzo and his supporters for the hanging of an archbishop, and calls on Florence to give him up. Florence does not. The Signoria and the Florentine clergy answer in writing, defending the man the Church has cut off and refusing the surrender outright. Two months after the cathedral, the quarrel is no longer between two families inside one city. Lorenzo stays in Florence. The bull is read out in Rome, and the answer to it is drafted in the Palazzo della Signoria.
suggested_refs: The Florentine synod's reply to the bull of 1 June 1478

stops.name: Santa Maria del Fiore, the city under interdict
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Wikipedia, 'Pazzi conspiracy': Florence placed under interdict on 20 June 1478).
stops.campa: The interdict shuts the sacraments to everybody in Florence. No Mass, no communion, no burial in consecrated ground, for wool-carders and Pazzi cousins alike, on account of one man's excommunication. The clergy of the city go on saying Mass regardless. In the same cathedral where Giuliano was killed eight weeks before, the punishment for punishing his killers now falls on the congregation. That summer the papal and Neapolitan armies cross the Florentine border.
suggested_refs: The interdict of 20 June 1478 and the Florentine clergy's refusal to observe it

stops.name: Palazzo della Signoria, the count of the dead
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Wikipedia, 'Pazzi conspiracy': eighty people executed between 26 April and 20 October 1478). The research pool cautions that the figure mixes formal trial, mob violence and summary killing, and that totals and their legal character vary by source. The pin is the seat of the government that carried out the repression, not a single execution site.
stops.campa: By the twentieth of October the reprisal has killed about eighty people. Some were tried, some were torn apart in the street, some were dispatched without either. The name Pazzi is abolished, the arms are cut off the walls they are carved on, the surviving men are imprisoned and the women are forbidden to marry. Lorenzo is twenty-nine. In six months he has buried his brother, been excommunicated and seen his city closed to the sacraments. He has been head of the house for nine years and holds no office in it.
suggested_refs: The Pazzi arms erased from Florentine buildings after 1478

stops.name: Palazzo del Capitano del Popolo, Bandini brought back
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Wikipedia, 'Pazzi conspiracy': hanged from a window of the Palazzo del Capitano del Popolo, 29 December 1479). Leonardo's sketch of the corpse is a well-known art-historical fact carried here from the research pool. Lorenzo himself was in Naples on that date.
stops.campa: Bernardo Bandini Baroncelli, who struck the first blow at Giuliano, had run as far as Constantinople. He is arrested there, handed over, and shipped back to Florence in irons. They hang him from a window of the Palazzo del Capitano del Popolo, still in the Turkish clothes he was taken in. Leonardo da Vinci stands in the crowd and draws him: the hang of the body, the set of the head, and beside the drawing a note of the colours of the dead man's cap, doublet and hose.
sources: Research pool on the extradition and Leonardo's sketch
suggested_refs: Leonardo da Vinci's drawing of the hanged Bernardo Bandini Baroncelli, Musee Bonnat, Bayonne

stops.name: Castel Nuovo, Lorenzo puts himself in Ferrante's hands
stops.date_confidence: Attested in outline, with a contradiction left standing. Wikipedia, 'Lorenzo de' Medici', calls him 'a prisoner of the king for several months'; the research pool frames the stay as a voluntary and calculated risk rather than confinement. Both accounts agree on the roughly three-month duration, December 1479 to March 1480, and on the outcome. Day defaulted to 01. The pool also warns against the myth that Lorenzo alone saved Italy by solitary eloquence.
stops.campa: With the papal and Neapolitan armies in Tuscany and the war going badly, he takes ship for Naples and walks into the court of Ferrante of Aragon, the same hall he was shown as a boy of sixteen. He is a guest, or he is a hostage. Nobody in Florence knows which, and it is not clear that he does. Ferrante keeps him about three months, feeding him, talking to him, letting the winter run. Whether the most famous journey of his life was an imprisonment or a wager is a question the sources have never settled.
sources: Research pool, 'War with the papacy and Naples, 1478-1480'
suggested_refs: The Sala dei Baroni of the Castel Nuovo, Naples

stops.name: Palazzo della Signoria, the return and the Seventy
stops.date_confidence: The return in March 1480 and the triumphal reception are attested in outline in the research pool and corroborated in general terms by Wikipedia. The creation of the Council of Seventy is dated 1480 in the pool from a summary of Florentine constitutional history and was not re-verified against a primary source. Day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He comes back in March with a settlement in his hand, and the city turns out along the road to meet him. The war ends. The alliance with Naples is remade, this time in his own name as much as the city's. Then the constitution is narrowed. A Council of Seventy is created, with standing committees for foreign affairs and for money. Every form of the republic is kept: the older councils still meet, still vote, and ratify what the Seventy have already settled among themselves. He is thirty-one.
stops.quote: Sappiate che chi dice male di noi non ci vuole bene.
stops.quote_source: Lorenzo de' Medici, saying reported by Francesco Guicciardini, Ricordi C 75, in Opere, ed. Roberto Palmarocchi (Bari: Laterza, 1933)
sources: Research pool, 'War with the papacy and Naples, 1478-1480'
suggested_refs: The Florentine reform of 1480 and the balie that created the Council of Seventy

stops.name: Florence, the reconciliation after Otranto
stops.date_confidence: The Ottoman capture of Otranto in 1480 and Florence's reconciliation with the papacy in the same year are carried in the research pool from a summary and were not re-verified in this pass. The pool assigns the ceremony to Florence and does not say where the envoys stood; the pin follows the pool. Month set to the summer of the Otranto landing; day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The Ottomans land at Otranto and take the town, and the shape of Italian politics turns south overnight. A crusade against Florence is indefensible while the Turk holds ground inside the kingdom of Naples. The interdict is lifted, the excommunication withdrawn, and Florentine representatives perform a formal act of submission for the hanging of the archbishop. Nobody in Italy wanted the invasion that made the reconciliation possible. The Ottomans hold Otranto for another year.
sources: Research pool, '1480-1484: Regional war and balance'
suggested_refs: The Ottoman occupation of Otranto, 1480-1481

stops.name: Palazzo Medici, the war over Ferrara kept at arm's length
stops.date_confidence: The Peace of Bagnolo was signed at Bagnolo Mella near Brescia on 7 August 1484 (it.wikipedia, 'Pace di Bagnolo'). Lorenzo was not there: the research pool flags that the peace was the product of diplomacy he directed from Florence, so this stop sits at his own pin rather than at the treaty site. CORRECTION of a reversed sequence in the pool: Sixtus IV died on 12 August 1484, FIVE DAYS AFTER the treaty and reportedly in a rage at terms he had not wanted, not before it.
stops.campa: Venice and the Pope go to war over Ferrara, and Lorenzo spends two years keeping Florence, Milan and Naples pointed the same way, by letter, from this house. He never sees the ground. What goes out of the door is paper, and what comes back is the news of other men's meetings. On the seventh of August the peace is signed at Bagnolo near Brescia, between Milan and Venice, on terms Sixtus had not wanted. The ambassadors read them out to him and he goes into a rage. Five days later he is dead.
sources: Research pool, '1480-1484: Regional war and balance'
suggested_refs: The text of the Peace of Bagnolo, 7 August 1484, between Milan and Venice

stops.name: Sarzanello, the fortress on the Ligurian border
stops.date_confidence: The Genoese garrison surrendered on 22 June 1487 after a siege begun in May (it.wikipedia, 'Sarzana'), which notes the garrison may have yielded on news of Lorenzo's imminent arrival, making his presence documented as imminent rather than merely unconfirmed. Coordinate corrected to the Fortezza di Sarzanello, 44.1151/9.9712, the entry's named place; the town itself lies at 44.1136/9.9600.
stops.campa: Sarzana commands the road between Tuscany and Genoa, and Florence means to have it back. The siege runs from May into late June. The garrison in the triangular fortress on the hill above the town gives up on the twenty-second, perhaps because word has reached them that Lorenzo is already on the road. He arrives to a place taken without him. His son Piero, fifteen, is with the army. Whether the Genoese gave up to the siege or to the news of a banker riding up from Florence is not recorded.
sources: Research pool, '1484-1489: Innocent VIII, family strategy and internal control'
suggested_refs: The Fortezza di Sarzanello above Sarzana

stops.name: Palazzo Medici, Clarice dies while he is away
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Wikipedia, 'Clarice Orsini': died of tuberculosis in Florence on 30 July 1488 and was buried two days later). CORRECTION: the research pool's geography lens staged this death at the Careggi villa, contradicting the pool's own chronology and the source, which both say Florence. Careggi is where Lorenzo died in 1492, not where Clarice died in 1488. Lorenzo's absence taking a cure is carried from the pool and is not primary-verified.
stops.campa: Clarice dies of consumption in Florence, in the house she came to as a Roman bride nineteen years ago. Lorenzo is away taking the waters for the gout and the arthritis that are already crippling him. He does not come back for it, and she is buried two days later. Their daughter Luisa died in May, betrothed and not grown. Of the ten children Clarice bore, four are already in the ground: the twins who lived a few days, Contessina Beatrice who lived a month, and now Luisa. The city ate at the wedding for four days.
stops.quote: il dolore è spesso sanza dolcezza, e la dolcezza non mai sanza dolore
stops.quote_source: Lorenzo de' Medici, Comento sopra alcuni de' suoi sonetti, p. 91, in Opere, ed. Attilio Simioni (Bari: Laterza, 1913), vol. I
suggested_refs: Clarice Orsini's burial in Florence, 1 August 1488

stops.name: Palazzo Medici, a cardinal at thirteen
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Wikipedia, 'Pope Leo X': created cardinal on 9 March 1489, aged 13, Lorenzo having prevailed on Innocent VIII, and barred from the insignia and from deliberations for three years). The creation was made at Rome; the pin is Lorenzo's own house, where he pressed for it and where the boy went on living. The Cybo marriage is attested by Wikipedia, 'Clarice Orsini'.
stops.campa: Innocent VIII, whose natural son Franceschetto Cybo is married to Lorenzo's daughter Maddalena, makes Lorenzo's second son Giovanni a cardinal at thirteen. The boy may not wear the insignia, sit in consistory or be published for three years. He is a schoolboy holding the second rank in Christendom in escrow. Lorenzo has bought his family a permanent seat inside the institution that excommunicated him eleven years ago, and has paid for it with a daughter.
stops.quote: il contento umano consiste più tosto nel parere che nell'essere
stops.quote_source: Lorenzo de' Medici, Comento sopra alcuni de' suoi sonetti, p. 91, in Opere, ed. Attilio Simioni (Bari: Laterza, 1913), vol. I
suggested_refs: The brief of Innocent VIII creating Giovanni de' Medici cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Dominica, 9 March 1489

segments.name: The Villas, the Garden, the Friar

stops.name: Poggio a Caiano, the villa on the Ombrone
stops.date_confidence: CORRECTION of the research pool's 'late 1480s': it.wikipedia, 'Villa medicea di Poggio a Caiano', puts Lorenzo's purchase and the commission to Giuliano da Sangallo between 1470 and 1474, with the villa only about a third built at his death in 1492. Coordinate corrected to 43.8175/11.0563; the value 43.8167/11.0667 in circulation is roughly 850 metres east. Date set to 1474 to order the segment.
stops.campa: Between Florence and Pistoia, on the low hill above the Ombrone, he buys the land in the early 1470s and sets Giuliano da Sangallo to work. The house rises on a barrel-vaulted podium behind a temple front, at the centre of a working estate of drained fields and imported cattle. Nothing like it has been built for a private man: the front of a temple on the front of a farm. He writes the poem Ambra about the river below it. At his death about a third of it stands.
sources: it.wikipedia, 'Villa medicea di Poggio a Caiano'

stops.name: Sassetti Chapel, Santa Trinita, the face from life
stops.date_confidence: The Sassetti Chapel cycle is dated 1483-1486 (Wikipedia, 'Sassetti Chapel'); 1485 is set here to order the segment and month and day are defaulted to 01. The identification of Lorenzo greeting Poliziano in the Confirmation of the Rule is the standard reading of the fresco. Valori's description is verified verbatim in the 1905 Janet Ross edition on the Internet Archive; the two sentences are not contiguous in that source.
stops.campa: Domenico Ghirlandaio paints the confirmation of the Franciscan rule on the wall of a banker's chapel, puts the Piazza della Signoria behind it and living Florentines in front of it. Lorenzo stands among them, dark, heavy-jawed, the flattened nose plain in the paint, with Poliziano and the Medici children coming up the stair towards him. It is a likeness made while the man is in the city to be looked at. Niccolò Valori, who knew him, wrote down what the fresco is too courteous to say.
stops.quote: Although nature had been a step-mother to him with regard to his personal appearance, she had acted as a loving mother in all things connected with the mind. ... Although his face was not handsome it was so full of dignity as to compel respect.
stops.quote_source: Niccolò Valori, quoted in Janet Ross, Florentine Palaces & Their Stories (1905), p. 250; the two sentences are separated in the source by a description of his complexion, flattened nose and absent sense of smell
sources: Janet Ross, Florentine Palaces & Their Stories (1905), p. 250 (Internet Archive item florentinepalace00ross)
suggested_refs: Ghirlandaio, Confirmation of the Franciscan Rule, Sassetti Chapel, Santa Trinita, Florence

stops.name: Villa Medici, Fiesole, the villa lent to Pico
stops.date_confidence: Coordinate corrected to 43.8057/11.2891. The villa was built for Giovanni de' Medici between 1451 and 1457 and was inherited, not built, by Lorenzo. Pico's residence there from 1488 to 1492 is attested on his own journey file. CORRECTIONS to the research pool: the pool's geography lens placed the Pico protection at Careggi and dated it 1490, and its chronology named Innocent VIII as the object of Lorenzo's intercession. The documented intercession was with Charles VIII of France, who released Pico from Vincennes; Innocent VIII allowed him to live in Florence but never lifted the censures, which stood until 1493, after Lorenzo's death. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, his theses condemned at Rome and himself arrested in France, is got out of the keep at Vincennes because Lorenzo sets every prince in Italy writing to Charles VIII. He comes to Florence and Lorenzo gives him the hillside villa above the city. There he writes the Heptaplus and dedicates it to the man who housed him, and De ente et uno after it. The censures are never lifted in Lorenzo's lifetime. What is on offer here is not a pardon; it is a wall, and it stands only while the man holding it up is alive.
suggested_refs: Pico della Mirandola, Heptaplus (1489), dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici

stops.name: Giardino di San Marco, the boy from Ghirlandaio's shop
stops.date_confidence: [R] The garden years are traditional rather than documented. Vasari (1550/1568) and Condivi (1553) are late and interested sources, and the research pool's safest reconstruction is roughly two years of late-adolescent patronage under Bertoldo di Giovanni's supervision, not the adoption of a child into the household. Michelangelo was seventeen when Lorenzo died. Date set to 1490 to order the segment.
stops.campa: Lorenzo asks Ghirlandaio for his two best apprentices and is given Francesco Granacci and a boy called Michelangelo Buonarroti. In the garden by San Marco, among the antique marbles, Bertoldo di Giovanni teaches them what he learned from Donatello. Michelangelo carves a faun's head and is brought to eat at the table on Via Larga with Ficino and Poliziano and two Medici children who will each become pope. He is there about two years. He is seventeen when Lorenzo dies.
sources: Research pool, '1489-1492: Pico, Michelangelo, Savonarola and last diplomacy'

stops.name: Convent of San Marco, the friar sent for
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Wikipedia, 'Girolamo Savonarola': Savonarola returned to Florence in May or June 1490 as lector at San Marco, Lorenzo having succeeded in bringing him back, with Pico persuading Lorenzo that the friar would bring prestige to the convent). Coordinate corrected to 43.7785/11.2590; the value 43.7764/11.2588 in circulation is about 230 metres south. Savonarola's refusal to pay court on Via Larga is Savonarolan biographical tradition, not documented.
stops.campa: Pico tells Lorenzo that a Dominican he once heard preach would bring credit to San Marco, and Lorenzo has him brought. Girolamo Savonarola arrives in the early summer as lector of the convent the Medici have paid to rebuild and to furnish. Inside two years he is its prior. He preaches against luxury, against tyrants, against the rich of the city. His own biographers say he never once came to the door of the house that sent for him. No document says he did, and none says he did not.
suggested_refs: The convent of San Marco, rebuilt at Cosimo de' Medici's expense by Michelozzo

stops.name: Villa Medici, Careggi, the house of the readers
stops.date_confidence: [R] The gatherings at Careggi are real but informal. The research pool follows Hankins in warning explicitly against the myth of a nightly Platonic Academy with fixed membership meeting here. Date set to 1485 to order the segment; month and day defaulted to 01. The motto is given in English in Del Lungo and Steegman (1907); the original-language wording behind that rendering was not traced.
stops.campa: The family villa stands in the hills a few miles north of the city, and Lorenzo rides up to it to read. Marsilio Ficino comes, and Poliziano, and Pico della Mirandola. Greek, Latin, argument, dinner. Later writers will furnish the place with an academy, statutes, fixed evenings and a roll of members, none of which existed. What existed was a house, a garden, a library and a handful of men who could read Plato in the original, meeting when the master of the house was free.
stops.quote_source: Lorenzo de' Medici's personal motto, as given in English in Del Lungo and Steegman, Women of Florence (1907), quoted on Wikiquote
sources: Research pool, 'Property, collections and building', citing Hankins on the Platonic Academy myth
suggested_refs: James Hankins, 'The Myth of the Platonic Academy of Florence'

stops.name: Villa Medici, Careggi, the friar at the bedside
stops.date_confidence: [R] Tradition, and contested; the contradiction is left standing. Savonarolan biography, from Fra Pacifico Burlamacchi onward, has the dying Lorenzo send for Savonarola, who exacts faith and restitution and then withholds absolution when Lorenzo will not restore Florentine liberty. Poliziano, writing as a contemporary, gives a quieter and more pious account with no three conditions. The Wikipedia article on Savonarola fetched for this file mentions no such meeting at all. A visit is plausible; the scripted dialogue is not established. Day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The story that has come down is a morality play: the friar at the foot of the bed, three demands, absolution refused over the third. Poliziano, who was in the house, wrote a letter describing something else, a death in order, confession made and the sacrament taken. Both accounts were set down by men with a case to argue, and the earliest life to carry the confrontation was written by a Savonarolan. What is not in doubt is that the friar was in Florence and that Lorenzo was dying.
sources: Research pool on the Savonarolan biographical tradition (Burlamacchi) versus Poliziano's contemporary letter
Wikipedia, 'Girolamo Savonarola' (silent on any such meeting)
suggested_refs: Poliziano's letter on the death of Lorenzo

stops.name: Villa Medici, Careggi, the death
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Wikipedia, 'Lorenzo de' Medici': died during the late night of 8 April 1492 at the family villa of Careggi, aged 43). The portents are Florentine chronicle tradition and are tagged [R] in the research pool. The retrospective diagnosis of acromegaly, argued by some modern medical historians from his symptoms, his skeleton and his death mask, is explicitly speculative and forms no part of the contemporary record.
stops.campa: He dies in the late night of the eighth of April, forty-three years old, in the family villa outside the walls. Gout has been eating at him for years, as it ate his father and his grandfather. Florentine chroniclers will write that lightning struck the dome of the cathedral that night, that ghosts were seen in the streets, that the Medici lions in their cages on the Via del Leone turned and fought each other. Two years later his son Piero is driven out of Florence.
stops.quote: Quant'è bella giovinezza, che si fugge tuttavia! Chi vuol esser lieto, sia: di doman non c'è certezza.
stops.quote_source: Lorenzo de' Medici, Trionfo di Bacco e Arianna (Canzona di Bacco), opening refrain; Italian as printed on Wikipedia, 'Trionfo di Bacco e Arianna'. No published English translator was traced for this refrain.

stops.name: Basilica di San Lorenzo, the sarcophagus in the Old Sacristy
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Wikipedia, 'Lorenzo de' Medici'; Wikipedia, 'Sagrestia Vecchia'): first buried alongside Giuliano in the porphyry and bronze tomb chest Verrocchio made for Piero and Giovanni de' Medici between 1469 and 1472, in the Old Sacristy. The day of burial is not given in any source fetched; 9 April is a placeholder to order the segment.
stops.campa: He is carried down from Careggi and laid with his murdered brother in the porphyry and bronze chest Verrocchio made for their father and their uncle, in the old sacristy Brunelleschi built. The Signoria of the republic that never gave him an office passes a decree over the body. Angelo Poliziano writes a Latin lament, Quis dabit capiti meo aquam, and Heinrich Isaac sets it to music before the year is out. In the setting, the tenor voice drops out at the point in the text where Lorenzo dies.
stops.quote: Whereas the foremost man of all this city, the lately deceased Lorenzo de' Medici, did, during his whole life, neglect no opportunity of protecting, increasing, adorning and raising this city...
stops.quote_source: Official decree of the Signoria of Florence after Lorenzo's death, quoted in Hugh Ross Williamson, Lorenzo the Magnificent (London: Michael Joseph, 1974), pp. 268-269
sources: Hugh Ross Williamson, Lorenzo the Magnificent (1974), pp. 268-269

stops.name: New Sacristy, San Lorenzo, the unmarked chest
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Wikipedia, 'Lorenzo de' Medici'; Wikipedia, 'New Sacristy'): the bodies of Lorenzo and Giuliano were moved into the New Sacristy in 1559 and placed in an unmarked tomb beneath Michelangelo's Madonna and Child. This postdates his life by sixty-seven years and is carried here as the resting place of his own body, not as a journey he made. Month and day defaulted to 01. CORRECTION to the research pool: the installation of the sculptures was Niccolò Tribolo's in 1545, finished by Vasari and Ammannati by 1555, not Vasari's alone.
stops.campa: Sixty-seven years on, the bones of the two brothers are moved a few yards into the room Michelangelo built for their descendants and put under the altar at the entrance wall, in a plain marble chest with no name cut into it. Above them stands his Madonna and Child, flanked by the Medici saints Cosmas and Damian. The great tomb intended for the brothers was never begun. Visitors cross the room to the seated duke in armour and take him for the Magnificent. He is the grandson and namesake, Duke of Urbino.
stops.quote: ...si governò sempre con tanta prudenzia e virtù che quella città ragionevolmente non si è mai ricordata sanza lacrime della sua immatura morte, perché a' tempi sua la fiorì di tutte quelle prosperità che può avere una città, di ricchezze, di imperio, di uomini virtuosi, di lettere e di tutte le arte buone, di reputazione, e sopra tutto di una grandissima unione e concordia civile.
stops.quote_source: Francesco Guicciardini, Elogio di Lorenzo de' Medici, in Scritti politici e ricordi, ed. Roberto Palmarocchi (Bari: Laterza, 1933), p. 229; text at it.wikisource. Leading ellipsis marks the subordinate opening. The Elogio is a retrospective assessment, not a 1492 utterance.
sources: it.wikisource, Guicciardini, Elogio di Lorenzo de' Medici
